name: Antegrade femoral nailing through a piriformis entry
corridor: Proximal gluteal split aligned with the femoral bow to a piriformis-fossa start just medial to the greater-trochanter tip

positioning.text: Position supine or lateral according to reduction strategy, with the pelvis accessible and the hip positioned to obtain true AP and lateral images of the proximal femur.

setup.text: Drape to the pelvic rim, plan reduction and traction, and verify that imaging can show the piriformis start, neck, canal, fracture, and distal femur before incision.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark the greater-trochanter tip, femoral axis, projected anatomic bow, and pelvic rim, using fluoroscopy when habitus obscures palpation.

incision.text: Make a 3–5 cm incision generally 10–15 cm proximal to the trochanter tip, farther proximal when habitus requires, aligned with the proximal extension of the femoral bow rather than horizontally.

superficial_interval.text: Open fascia in line with the incision and split gluteal fibers longitudinally, maintaining a collinear soft-tissue path to bone.

deep_interval.text: Palpate the trochanter and place the guidewire at the piriformis fossa just medial to the trochanter tip under AP and lateral fluoroscopy.

layers.text: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, fascia lata/gluteal fascia, gluteal muscle split, piriformis-fossa cortex, then femoral canal.

structures_encountered.text: Gluteal fascia and muscle, greater trochanter, piriformis-fossa region, proximal femoral cortex, neck-adjacent bone, and medullary canal define the entry.

structures_at_risk.text: The superior gluteal nerve and vessels, femoral-neck cortex, abductor tissue, proximal femoral cortex, and posterior shaft cortex are at risk from a noncollinear track.

danger_zones.text: A too-distal skin portal or oblique guidewire causes eccentric reaming, medial cortical blowout, posterior perforation, or iatrogenic femoral-neck fracture.

retraction_hazards.text: Avoid forceful lateral retraction that bends the soft-tissue track; lengthen the incision proximally to achieve collinearity rather than levering instruments against the trochanter.

exposure.text: Provides a direct start for straight antegrade nails aligned closely with the femoral canal while limiting fracture-site exposure.

limitations.text: The piriformis start can be technically difficult in obesity and demands precise positioning; comparative trials do not show universal clinical superiority over trochanteric entry.

extensions.text: Extend the proximal skin and muscle split to restore a collinear trajectory; use a reduction window at the fracture only when closed methods fail.

indications.text: Use for selected femoral shaft or distal-third fractures treated with a compatible straight antegrade nail and a safe piriformis start.

relative_contraindications.text: Favor another entry when body habitus, proximal anatomy, prior implants, hip disease, or nail design prevents safe collinear piriformis access.

implant_implications.text: Use only a nail designed for piriformis entry and maintain the guidewire, opening reamer, and nail along the canal to avoid neck or cortical stress.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Confirm the start and guidewire on true AP and lateral views, then monitor centered reaming, fracture alignment, nail depth, and proximal and distal locking.

closure.text: Irrigate, confirm hemostasis, repair fascia without tethering abductors, and close subcutaneous tissue and skin.

complications.text: Complications include superior-gluteal or abductor injury, hip pain, eccentric reaming, trochanteric or neck fracture, cortical perforation, malalignment, nonunion, and infection.

bailouts.text: If the start cannot be made collinear, stop repeated reaming, reposition or extend proximally, or change to a compatible trochanteric or retrograde strategy.

procedure_applications.condition: An antegrade straight nail is selected and proximal anatomy permits a collinear piriformis-fossa start

questions.question: Where is the piriformis entry point?
questions.answer: Just medial to the tip of the greater trochanter and aligned with the femoral canal.

questions.question: Why is a distal skin incision dangerous?
questions.answer: It creates an oblique track that promotes eccentric reaming and cortical or femoral-neck injury.

questions.question: Which nail geometry uses this entry?
